quote: The duration of analgesia and of hypoaesthesia produced by a variety of solutions has been examined by skin weal testing; each separate study was carried out in twenty female volunteers under double-blind conditions.
proposed_wording: A double-blind volunteer trial has timed prilocaine with adrenaline injected intradermally: in 20 female volunteers the mean duration of analgesia was 288.7 min (SE 10.2) and the mean duration of hypoaesthesia 349.1 min (SE 13.2) (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).
reason: The full text answers the open question yes on every element. Prilocaine 1 per cent with adrenaline was one of six coded solutions each given as a 0.25 ml intradermal skin weal in the ventral left forearm of 20 female volunteers under double-blind conditions, and both timed endpoints were recorded for it: duration of analgesia 288.7 min and duration of hypoaesthesia 349.1 min, against 99.1 min and 172.9 min for the same prilocaine solution without adrenaline. The claim's elements - humans, prilocaine with epinephrine, any study, duration of anaesthesia, injected into skin - are all matched, so the claim is refuted rather than confirmed.

quote: The duration of analgesia and of hypoaesthesia produced by a variety of solutions has been examined by skin weal testing; each separate study was carried out in twenty female volunteers under double-blind conditions.
proposed_wording: Human intradermal studies have timed prilocaine more than once (Padfield 1967; Swerdlow and Jones 1970; Reynolds 1976; Willatts and Reynolds 1985), and the 1970 double-blind volunteer trial does report mean durations per concentration: plain prilocaine 99.1 min of analgesia and 172.9 min of hypoaesthesia, the double-strength solution 100.8 min and 244.5 min, and prilocaine with adrenaline 288.7 min and 349.1 min, in 20 volunteers.
reason: The claim says nobody has timed a prilocaine wheal in human skin beyond Willatts and Reynolds 1985, and that that study gives no mean per concentration. Swerdlow and Jones 1970 timed prilocaine 1 per cent and 2 per cent, and prilocaine 1 per cent with adrenaline, as 0.25 ml intradermal weals in 20 female volunteers, and reports a mean duration with a standard error for each - so both halves of the claim fail. It also cites Padfield 1967, an earlier controlled double-blind intradermal prilocaine study. The existing refuted verdict stands and the full text removes the uncertainty behind it.

proposed_wording: A human head-to-head duration comparison in minutes on a skin endpoint exists: a 1970 double-blind volunteer trial timed prilocaine against bupivacaine and lignocaine in intradermal weals in the same 20 subjects and reported mean durations in minutes with standard errors and significance tests (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413). The horse study remains the only one reporting those figures with confidence intervals.
reason: The claim, and the source note behind it, say the only head-to-head duration figures in minutes on a skin endpoint come from a study in horses. Swerdlow and Jones 1970 matches every element of that scope: a comparative study, a cutaneous (intradermal weal) sensory endpoint, prilocaine head to head against two other local anaesthetics in the same subjects, and durations reported in minutes as means with standard errors plus significance tests between agents. Only the claim's unstated preference for confidence intervals keeps the horse study distinctive, so the uniqueness claim is refuted.

quote: Adrenaline significantly lengthened the action of all three drugs, this prolongation being greatest with lignocaine.
proposed_wording: More than five measurements put numbers on prilocaine's duration and they disagree. Those that bear on a wheal include a 1970 double-blind human intradermal trial reporting means in minutes for plain prilocaine, for the double-strength solution and for prilocaine with adrenaline (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413); further figures come from spinal, epidural, dental and nerve-block use, and they also disagree.
reason: The claim counts five measurements of prilocaine's duration. Swerdlow and Jones 1970 is a further one, and unlike the spinal, epidural and dental figures already recorded against this claim it is intradermal, so it bears directly on a wheal rather than only adding to the off-route total. It supplies three more prilocaine duration means (plain, double strength, and with adrenaline), which widens the spread the claim rests on. The narrowing stands and the existing proposed wording needs correcting, because it says the measurements bearing on a wheal are only those five.

proposed_wording: Swerdlow and Jones 1970 has now been read: it holds human intradermal duration data for bupivacaine, lignocaine and prilocaine each with and without adrenaline, for hospital-prepared against commercially prepared solutions of all three with adrenaline, and for intradermal saline with and without adrenaline. Its prilocaine-with-adrenaline arm and its preparation comparison have not been found elsewhere; the plain-versus-adrenalized intradermal comparison has been repeated since for lidocaine and bupivacaine (Howe and Williams 1994; Liu 1995), neither of which included prilocaine.
reason: This claim names Swerdlow and Jones 1970 as one of the unopened papers said to carry human intradermal data existing nowhere else. The full text shows the repeat studies cited against it do not cover all of what it holds: Howe 1994 and Liu 1995 repeated the plain-versus-adrenalized intradermal comparison for lidocaine and bupivacaine but neither used prilocaine, and neither compared hospital-prepared with commercially prepared solutions. The narrowing therefore holds only for the lidocaine and bupivacaine part, and the paper is no longer unopened.

Swerdlow and Jones 1970 timed plain bupivacaine, lignocaine and prilocaine as intradermal weals to the point at which the sensory change had completely disappeared, and plain bupivacaine ran 306.8 min at single and 435.8 min at double strength - long, not short - so the 'all four ran short' half does not hold once this study is counted. The weal volume, 0.25 ml, is above the 0.05-0.1 ml range the page means by a wheal, so the claim is narrowed rather than refuted. proposed_wording: No study has measured plain intradermal bupivacaine at [dose figure omitted]. A 1970 double-blind volunteer trial did time plain bupivacaine in intradermal weals to complete recovery of sensation, 306.8 min at single and 435.8 min at double strength, but at a volume above the wheal range this page uses (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).
reason: The claim has two parts: nothing measured plain intradermal bupivacaine at the page's smallest wheal volume, and neither interpolated study was timed to complete recovery at a wheal volume. Swerdlow and Jones 1970 does time plain bupivacaine intradermally to complete recovery of sensation, in 20 volunteers under double-blind conditions, but at 0.25 ml, which is outside the 0.05-0.1 ml volume element the claim sets, so the claim is not refuted and stays confirmed. The remaining uncertainty is about the volumes used by Reynolds 1976 and Morgan 1975, which this paper does not settle.

proposed_wording: Willatts and Reynolds 1985 holds the only human intradermal duration data for six drugs at once. It is not the only source of concentration-duration data in human skin: a 1970 double-blind volunteer trial timed bupivacaine, lignocaine and prilocaine each at two concentrations in intradermal weals and tested the difference for each agent (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).
reason: The claim bundles two uniqueness statements: intradermal duration data for six drugs at once, and the concentration-duration slopes. The first holds - this paper used three agents. The second does not: its third trial gave 20 volunteers double-strength solutions of all three agents and compared the durations of analgesia and of hypoaesthesia against the single-strength results agent by agent, with significance tests, which is human intradermal concentration-duration data. The claim is therefore narrowed to the six-drugs-at-once part.

proposed_wording: Collins 2013 is the only human intradermal study of lidocaine with epinephrine at the drug and epinephrine strengths it names ([dose figure omitted]). Todd 1992 timed intradermal lidocaine with epinephrine at four body sites at an epinephrine strength its abstract does not state, and a 1970 double-blind volunteer trial timed lignocaine with adrenaline in intradermal weals in 20 volunteers at a different adrenaline strength (Swerdlow and Jones 1970, PMID 4913413).
reason: The claim calls Collins 2013 the only human study using the intradermal route with that drug and that epinephrine strength. Swerdlow and Jones 1970 is another human intradermal study of the same drug with adrenaline, timed to both return of sensation and complete recovery, but at a different adrenaline strength, so the uniqueness survives only because it is pinned to that exact strength. The narrowing stands; the open question already attached to this claim asks what epinephrine strength Todd 1992 used, which this paper does not answer.

quote: No previous similar trial has been found
proposed_wording: Padfield 1967 is an earlier controlled double-blind intradermal study of prilocaine compared with lignocaine and procaine in man (PMID 6054556), so human intradermal timing of prilocaine predates Willatts and Reynolds 1985 by nearly two decades.
reason: Working the reference list turned up Padfield 1967, 'The intradermal local analgesic action of prilocaine. A controlled double-blind comparison with lignocaine and procaine' (Anaesthesia; PMID 6054556, DOI 10.1111/j.1365-2044.1967.tb10153.x). Its title alone matches the claim's elements - humans, prilocaine injected intradermally, a controlled study, local analgesic action - so it independently refutes the claim that Willatts and Reynolds 1985 is the only human intradermal prilocaine study. Swerdlow and Jones cite it as the only previous similar trial they could find, and report that it also found intradermal saline produced a brief period of analgesia. The record has no abstract, so its durations in minutes cannot be read without the full text.
